# How FOG OF SEA works

FOG OF SEA is a fictional six-turn planning game. You first identify what the
mission requires, choose a strategic approach, and assemble a force. During
command, you choose how that force moves, senses, coordinates, manages risk,
and acts.

## How a scenario is accepted

A complete candidate must pass the game's implemented structured coexistence
checks before it appears. Those checks compare such fields as region, season,
light, weather, sea, geography, mission, actors, force needs, objectives, and
the difficulty matrix. Passing them does not prove that every accepted problem
is winnable, nontrivial, doctrinally sound, or politically coherent, and it
does not validate every implication of narrative prose.

## What to watch during a turn

- **Range** tells you how far the force is from the problem.
- **Contact quality** tells you how confidently the force understands what it
  is observing.
- **Integrity, readiness, and supply** tell you whether the force can keep
  operating.
- **Objective progress** tells you whether the mission is advancing.
- **Escalation** tells you how much political and operational danger the
  approach is creating.

Your selected orders change several of these at once. Faster or more forceful
choices can advance the mission, but may consume supply, weaken the force, or
raise escalation. Cautious choices can preserve the force, but may lose time or
fail to create enough progress.

## How to read the opposition

Turn 1 establishes the command baseline. Before resolving each later turn,
you must record three working judgments: what the opposition may want, what
the observable pattern may mean, and what the opposition may do next. Each
menu is limited to a small set supported by the picture already available to
you and always includes an insufficient-evidence choice.

These judgments are hypotheses for reflection. They are saved in the turn
record, but they do not change the umpire, the score, or what becomes visible.
The menus refer to the opposition in aggregate and do not reveal whether the
hidden scenario contains one or several actors.

The left intelligence panel separates facts from potentials. **Absolutely
known** contains current invented strike-group indices and only those opposing
actions whose observation rule has been met. **Immediate** contains the latest
absolutely known opposing action plus inflictions and discoveries available
for the current decision. Infliction values are invented game effects, not
real-world battle-damage assessments.

**History** includes every resolved turn. A fact is filed under the turn when
it occurred. If the strike group confirms it later, the earlier turn gains a
**Discovered during Turn N** group; the event is not moved to the later turn
or rewritten as though it was known earlier.

## How a turn is resolved

The game considers the accepted scenario, environment, selected force, current
state, and your orders. It applies the same fixed rules to that saved state.
Repeating the same saved state and orders produces the same result; Undo is for
comparison, not rerolling.

The ordinary turn screen does not explain a result before it happens. After a
turn, its collapsed report shows what changed and reports a tracked task,
reach, contact, or employment mismatch; a committed matrix failure; or that no
tracked turn mismatch was recorded. The last state is not proof that every
requirement was met.

The final review presents each recorded diagnostic finding with its evidence
and one useful adjustment. When there is no final finding, it says only that no
tracked finding was recorded; that is not proof that every requirement was met
or that the plan was optimal. A committed matrix failure may also be reported
without being described as a hidden rule or a proven player error.

Some uncertainty is prepared when the scenario is created. That prevents a
player from obtaining a different result simply by repeating the same turn.
Those hidden commitments are checked when a save or TXT record is imported.
They are not instructions for real-world planning and are not shown as measured
odds during ordinary play.

Readable TXT records follow the same as-known boundary. Hidden actions,
committed draws, internal matrix notes, and unrevealed objectives remain out of
the readable log; the restorable machine block is encoded, not encrypted.

## How explanatory copy is prepared

Selected Field Guide, post-resolution, and Academy interface copy is compiled
before release through a pinned Lattice workflow. The browser receives only the
selected text; it does not run the Lattice engine or use it to decide rules,
scores, contacts, saves, or quiz answers. Automated copy checks do not establish
human approval, complete Academy sourcing, or universal accessibility.

## What the game does not judge

Free-form writing is for your own reasoning and export. It is not evaluated and
never changes the score. Results follow the model's invented rules, recorded
game state, and selected orders. All ranges, capacities, forces, and outcomes
belong to the fictional model and are not real-world predictions or
recommendations.
